newsitem.title: UK: Huge security operation over N Irish march.
newsitem.headline: Huge security operation over N Irish march.

text.p: British forces surged into an Irish Catholic enclave early on Sunday in one of the biggest security operations mounted in 28 years of Northern Ireland conflict.
In the dead of night, scores of stone-grey police Land Rovers rolled slowly down a half-mile (0.8 km) length of highway which forms one of the province's most bitterly disputed territories.
The trouble erupted after weeks of controversy over plans by the exclusively Protestant Orange Order to hold an annual parade through the zone later on Sunday .

Hundreds of riot police and soldiers were involved in the operation, which was almost unparalleled in a built-up, highly-populated zone. "I have never seen anything like it. It is mammoth," one reporter said.
A phalanx of police officers of the 92 percent Protestant Royal Ulster Constabulary advanced around 3 am (0200 gmt) along a gentle slope descending gradually to an avenue of chaos.
They wore full body protective gear -- zip-up, fire-resistant body suits with balaclavas attached, anti-riot pads on their legs and arms and back helmets with visors down.
Eyewitnesses said around 80 Catholics were at one end of the Garvaghy Road as the police pushed forward.

They said some of the Catholic protesters sat on the road but the officers kept advancing, raising their see-through riot shields to fend off a hail of bottles and stones hurled by youngsters on the pavement.
Around six petrol bombs trailed flames across the night air and exploded among the police vehicles.

Witnesses said a number of the protesters were hit with batons. The Land Rovers trundled bumper-to-bumper behind the advancing police as rioting erupted until they lined the entire 400-yard (metre) length of the flashpoint road.
Plastic bullets, which security forces frequently use during Northern Ireland clashes, were fired, showering sparks and smoke.
Down the centre of the road, as the rioters scattered into a maze of side streets, came around 20 armoured personnel carriers. They disgorged soldiers in full combat gear and carrying rifles.
As rioting continued, lines of police and army "snatch squads" confronted the crowds of teenagers, driving them back from the main road.
The clashes subsided as dawn broke, revealing the full panoply of armoured vehicle power along the disputed roadway.
By 0730 GMT, crowds were still milling about deep in the heart of the sprawling estate where the town's 6,000 minority Catholics live.
Catholics said they were uncertain whether they would be allowed to come out of the enclave to attend Sunday Mass.
